checkpoints.question: Every test today is written `async ({ page }) => { ... }`. What is that `page`?
options: A fresh browser tab, created for this test alone
One shared browser tab that every test in the file takes turns using
The page object for the site under test, which you define yourself
checkpoints.explanation: Each test gets its own `page` — a fresh tab, so nothing one test does leaks into the next. That per-test isolation was [Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1), and Day 5 of this week is about what happens when you split a test and lose it.

1.recap: Today's code uses the TypeScript from Week 1. If the table above had any surprises in it, follow the link before starting [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d1/p2) — the Playwright will be easier to see if the language underneath it is not also new.

checkpoints.question: You are filling a search box that shows autocomplete suggestions as you type, and the suggestions are what you need to click. Which method fills it?
options: `.fill()` — it is the default, and faster
`.pressSequentially()`, because the page reacts to each keystroke
Either — they produce identical events, only at different speeds
checkpoints.explanation: `.fill()` sets the value directly, so a page listening for per-key events never hears them and the suggestions never appear. That is exactly the case the lesson reserves `.pressSequentially()` for — it costs you the speed (68ms vs 92ms measured here) and you spend it deliberately.

checkpoints.question: On `#Skills` you call `.selectOption({ label: "Java" })`, then `.selectOption({ label: "Python" })`. What is selected at the end?
options: Both Java and Python — it has 78 options and takes multiple
Java only — the first pick wins and later calls are ignored
Neither — the second call throws, because the option is already taken
checkpoints.explanation: "Select Skills" reads like a multi-select and has 78 options, but it carries no `multiple` attribute — verified in the lesson. A single-select keeps only your last pick, so Python replaces Java silently. Nothing errors, which is what makes it worth knowing.

checkpoints.question: The spec at the end of this lesson reports `1 passed`. What has it actually proved?
options: That the form accepted the data and the registration succeeded
That every locator matched and no line threw — nothing more
That the page navigated away after Submit
checkpoints.explanation: There is not one `expect()` in that file, so "passed" means only that nothing threw on the way through. It is the same gap [Week 1 - Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) showed with a wrong password, and [Day 2](/learn/w2/d2/p2) is where you close it.

2.recap:
- `.fill()` by default. `.pressSequentially()` only when the page reacts to each keystroke.
- `.check()` makes a control checked — it does not toggle it, so calling it twice is safe and you never compute the current state first.
- `.selectOption({ label })` matches the visible text; a bare string matches the option's `value`.
- Verify a skinned `<select>` rather than assuming. `#country` carries `aria-hidden` and a Select2 class and still takes `.selectOption()` — on another app it might not.
- **A test with no `expect()` cannot fail for the right reason.** Everything today is actions; assertions start tomorrow.

checkpoints.question: The helper is saved as `registration-helpers.ts`, deliberately not `registration-helpers.spec.ts`. Why does the suffix matter?
options: The runner collects every `*.spec.ts` file and would try to execute a file with no tests in it
TypeScript refuses to export a function from a `.spec.ts` file
It is only a naming convention — either name works identically
checkpoints.explanation: The spec suffix is what the runner globs for. A helper that carries it gets collected and executed as a test file, and a file with no `test()` calls in it is an error, not a pass. The rule gets named formally in week 3.

checkpoints.question: Why does `fillRegistrationForm` take `email` as a parameter, but keep the first name, address and phone hardcoded?
options: Because strings are the only type a helper can safely accept
Because the email is the one value these tests actually need to differ — parameterizing the rest would add knobs nobody turns
Because Playwright requires every helper to take exactly one parameter beyond `page`
checkpoints.explanation: Two tests register two learners, and the only thing that has to differ between them is the email. Everything else is fixed on purpose. Problem 3 asks you to add the phone as a second parameter — because there the tests do need it to vary.

3.recap:
- Repetition across tests is a structural problem, not a typing problem: ten lines in thirty specs is thirty edits when the form changes.
- The fix is the simplest thing that works — a function. The Page Object Model is the same instinct with a class around it, and it arrives in week 3.
- Name a helper for what it does (`fillRegistrationForm`), not for the calls inside it.
- No `expect()` inside a helper that performs actions. That is a preview of the "no assertions in a page object" rule, and it holds for the same reason.
